units: the frame that carries the roof can be timber or steel
this frame passes the weight of the roof down to the load-bearing walls
thin strips of wood are nailed crosswise to take the covering
the covering described is a dark rock split into flat leaves
this covering lets the space under the roof breathe
a channel set at the foot of the slope catches the rainwater
this water is then sent into a vertical downpipe
an opening cut through the slope lights and airs the floor under the roof
this opening weakens the weathertight skin if it is badly fitted
a trained tradesman checks the whole of it before the wet months
text: A roof is an assembly of parts, and every one of them does a job you can name. The frame comes first, timber or steel, holding the whole thing up and handing the weight down to the walls that carry the load. Onto that frame go the battens, slim strips nailed crosswise, ready to take the covering. Slate does the covering here, a dark rock that splits into flat leaves, shedding rain while it lets the space beneath breathe. Along the foot of the slope a gutter catches what streams off and feeds it into a downpipe, so the face of the building stays dry. Higher up, a dormer cuts through the pitch to bring light and air into the room under the roof, and its surround has to be fitted closely, since any hole weakens the skin that keeps the water out. Before the wet months, a trained roofer goes over each of these parts.

units: the workmen were taking up a damaged floor at the top of an empty house
a workman's tool struck something hard under a board
an old timber covered with notches came to light
the man in charge of the site halted the work
a restoration specialist came to look at the find the next day
she recognized marks cut by the builder who raised the house
these marks showed in what order the structure had to be put together
the owner gave up the idea of replacing the structure
he chose instead to have it strengthened
the timber is left in view and protected by a pale coating
text: The work began on the top floor of a house nobody had lived in for two winters, where a rotten floor was coming up board by board. Under the third plank the workman felt his bar strike something that would not give. He brushed the dust away and uncovered an old beam, blackened, its hidden face cut with a row of even notches. The foreman stopped the job on the spot. A restorer of old buildings arrived the next morning. She ran her palm along the grain, recognized joining marks scored by the carpenter who had raised the house, and said they told whoever came later in what order the frame went back together. Each piece had been marked before it was lifted, the way words are numbered in a sentence taken apart. The owner, told at the end of the week, dropped the idea of replacing the frame and asked for it to be strengthened. The beam still shows overhead under a pale wax.

units: you have to check how wet the wall is before putting up a light partition
a damp backing keeps the covering from holding
the skim coat lifts away in flakes at the first heating if the backing is wet
the layout line is marked with a taut string
a floor track out of level throws off every upright and ripples the finish
the bonding compound is mixed in small amounts because it stiffens fast
a screw driven too deep tears the face and weakens the board
tape bedded onto a wet joint swells and then splits
a gap left at the foot of the partition keeps rising damp off it
text: Before you put up a light partition, take a moisture reading on the wall behind it. Plaster will not grip a damp backing, and the skim coat lifts away in flakes as soon as the heating comes on. Snap the layout line with a taut string, then set the floor track down: run it out of level and every upright inherits the error, so the finished face ripples along its length. Mix the bonding compound in small batches, since it stiffens fast and whatever is left over goes to waste. Drive each screw until the head sits flush and no deeper, because a torn face weakens the very board it was meant to hold. Let the work dry before you skim. Tape bedded onto a wet joint swells first and splits later, which shows through the paint. Leave a gap along the bottom edge as well, or the first trace of rising damp will stain the foot of the wall you have just built.

units: neighbours in a low-lying district had their cellars flooded after heavy rain
the trouble had been going on since the end of summer
a survey was ordered by the local authority
the drainage system had been laid out for ground that soaked up water
yards covered in concrete have done away with that soaking
the water reached the doorways of the houses and worked under the doors
the paths will be laid with a loose stony material that lets water through
channels running along the walls will carry the water to a basin dug further off
the money comes from a grant and from a share paid by the owners
a first stretch will be finished before the rainy season
text: Since the close of summer, people living in a low-lying district have reported cellars under water after every heavy downpour. A survey ordered by the local authority put the blame on the drainage system, laid out for ground that once soaked up the rain. Yard after yard has been covered in concrete, and nothing sinks in any more: the run-off slides toward the doorsteps and works its way under the doors. Two measures have now been settled on. The paths will be lifted and laid again with loose gravel, which lets rain pass through instead of throwing it back against the buildings. Stone channels will then follow the exposed walls and carry the flow to a holding basin dug well away from the houses. A grant to the authority covers most of the cost, with the owners paying the rest between them. One stretch is due before the rains come.

units: two houses look at each other from either side of a narrow street
they have nothing in common
the house on the left has a pale render on its walls
its openings are closed by painted wooden panels
over each opening on the left runs an oak lintel left in view
the house on the right has stone walls left bare
its openings are narrower and capped with a lintel of hard rock
it is shut by metal slats that slide rather than swing
the first gives a sense of welcome, the second a sense of closure
the doorsteps differ too, one of wood hollowed by use, the other a heavy slab
text: Two houses stand across a narrow street from each other, and they share nothing at all. The one on the left wears a pale lime render, broken by tall windows that painted wooden shutters close at dusk. Over every one of those windows sits an oak lintel left in plain view, barely curved, softening the flat run of the wall. The house opposite answers with bare stone, its joints raked deep, its openings pinched narrower and capped with a thick block of granite. No shutter swings there. Metal slats run down instead, sliding in a groove cut for them. The first house looks open-handed, a little worn by weather. The second looks shut, heavy, cut to stand up to the wind that comes along the street. Even the doorsteps part company, a wooden one hollowed by generations of feet on one side, a cold and heavy slab on the other.

units: the writer holds that we pull buildings down too readily instead of repairing them
his first charge is the waste of materials that could still be used
taking a building apart with care costs more than knocking it down quickly
his second charge concerns the loss of hand skills
these skills die out along with the places that passed them on
his third charge is aimed at the disappointing comfort of new buildings
the new building bakes in the warm season and whistles in the cold one
the bill lands on whoever lives in the place
his fourth charge is that what the occupants feel for the place counts for nothing
he is not asking that everything be kept but wants proof that no repair was possible
text: Let us be blunt: we knock buildings down far too fast and mend them far too rarely. Charge one, the waste. Sound roof timbers, tiles good for another lifetime, an oak staircase, all of it goes into the skip because taking a house apart with care costs more than swinging a bucket at it. Charge two, the hands that knew how. Who can still point a wall with lime, ease a sagging lintel back up, split a slate without cracking it? Those skills go out with the workshops that handed them on. Charge three, the comfort we were promised never turns up. What goes up in their place bakes in the warm months, whistles in the cold ones, and whoever lives there pays for both. Charge four, what people feel about a place they have lived in weighs nothing at all in the decision. I am not asking that everything be kept. Show me first that no serious repair was possible.

units: the woman in question was brought up beside a place where rock is quarried
her father worked there cutting stone out of the ground
she watched blocks being split before she split them herself
she went into training in a workshop that repairs old buildings
her first commission of note was cutting a fresh doorstep to replace a worn one
she went on to harder work, a cracked lintel and a vault to reset
she opened a workshop of her own about ten years after she started
she employs two workmen
she now teaches beginners, several of whom had never used a tool
she holds that this material calls for patience
text: A quarryman's daughter, the stone carver grew up beside a limestone pit, watching blocks come apart under the wedge long before she held a chisel of her own. At sixteen she took a place in a workshop that repairs old buildings, learned to read the grain of a block, and landed her first real commission, cutting a fresh doorstep for a roadside inn whose own had worn hollow. Harder work followed, a cracked lintel to make good, a vault to reset stone by stone. Ten winters or so after she began, she opened a workshop of her own and took on two men. Lately she gives part of every week to beginners from every sort of background, several of whom had never picked up a tool. Stone, she says, forgives impatience very badly, and what she really teaches them is how to slow the hand down.

units: the visitor leaves this refitted building feeling hemmed in
the feeling comes from choices of construction rather than from a quarrel over taste
an insulating skin has been added in front of the old walls
this addition has sunk the windows into a deep recess
the view outward is now blocked
a stretched ceiling hides the timber frame that used to be in view
hiding it takes away the sense of size the place had
the floor of loose stone has been replaced by a smooth surface
this surface throws sound back and makes the noise hard to bear
the reviewer approves of keeping the doorstep worn down by passing feet
text: You come out of this refitted hall short of breath, and the reason has less to do with taste than with what was built. The old walls have been lined throughout with an insulating skin, which drops each window to the end of a deep shaft, so the eye runs aground well before it reaches the daylight. The roof frame, once readable from one end of the hall to the other, has gone behind a stretched ceiling, and with it went the measure that made the room feel generous. The floor of packed gravel gave way to a smooth screed, which throws every voice back off bare surfaces and turns ordinary talk into a din. One decision consoles. The doorstep was kept as it was, worn into a hollow by feet beyond counting, a reminder that the place was in use before anyone thought to improve it.

units: the writer is addressing his neighbour in writing
he brings up the channel that catches water along the wall they share
this channel has been spilling over since the recent rains
the water is eating into the wall covering and laying the mortar bare
a look at it showed a blockage of leaves and an empty nest
one fixing bracket has given way and tipped part of the channel over
the writer offers to clear the channel himself shortly
he offers to replace the broken brackets and put the fall right
he suggests fitting a guard so that the trouble does not come back
he asks his neighbour whether she agrees to all this
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing about the gutter that runs along the wall our two houses share. Since last week's downpours it has been spilling over halfway down its length, and the water is eating into the render, which is going soft and letting the mortar show through. I put a ladder up to look at it. The channel is packed with matted leaves and an abandoned nest, and one of the brackets has given way, which tips that whole length backward. Three things would sort it out. A thorough clear-out first, and I can do that myself before the week is over. Then the two broken brackets replaced, cheap enough as parts go, with the fall eased a little toward the downpipe. Last, a guard over the mouth of the channel so that the same thing does not build up again. Tell me whether that suits you.

units: the text sets timber-frame building against building in concrete
the comparison comes up when a client looks at two tenders
timber goes up fast because the parts are shaped in the workshop beforehand
its lightness allows shallower foundations
timber suffers from water and calls for wide roof overhangs
the points where timber meets the ground need watching closely
concrete stores warmth and flattens the swings of temperature
it also cuts down the noise from outside
making it costs the environment dearly and its drying stretches the work out
the common answer joins a concrete base to a timber frame
text: Timber frame or concrete? The question comes up the moment a client sets two tenders side by side. What does timber offer? Speed above all, since the parts arrive shaped from the workshop, the site stays clean, and a light structure sits happily on shallow foundations. What is held against it? Water. Timber wants a roof that oversails well beyond the walls, and every point where it meets the ground has to be watched year after year. What does concrete offer? Mass, which soaks up warmth, flattens the swing between day and night, and muffles the noise coming off the street. What is held against it? A heavy toll in the making, and drying times that stretch the work out. So which of them wins? Very often both, a solid base carrying a light frame, a pairing that serves the building better than either on its own.
